name: minerals

description.en: The formulas of 40 common minerals and the hardness of the ten Mohs reference minerals, in 50 cards. Forty cards show a mineral's name in English and Swedish on the front and its ideal chemical formula on the back, written with subscripts (quartz SiO₂, calcite CaCO₃). Ten cards ask for the hardness, from 1 to 10, of the ten reference minerals of the Mohs scale. The formulas come from Wikidata, checked against the IMA list of minerals, and the hardness values from the US Geological Survey. The Swedish names were checked against Svenska Akademiens ordböcker, SGU and the Swedish Wikipedia.
description.sv: Formlerna för 40 vanliga mineral och hårdheten hos Mohs tio referensmineral, på 50 kort. Fyrtio kort har mineralets namn på engelska och svenska på framsidan och dess idealformel på baksidan, skriven med nedsänkta siffror (kvarts SiO₂, kalkspat CaCO₃). Tio kort frågar efter hårdheten, från 1 till 10, hos de tio referensmineralen i Mohs hårdhetsskala. Formlerna kommer från Wikidata, kontrollerade mot IMA:s mineralförteckning, och hårdheterna från USA:s geologiska undersökning (USGS). De svenska namnen är kontrollerade mot Svenska Akademiens ordböcker, SGU och svenskspråkiga Wikipedia.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (a script comparing each formula's element composition with Wikidata and the IMA list, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Candidates: a list of about 75 minerals met in school chemistry and geology (common rock-forming minerals, ore minerals, evaporites, carbonates, gemstone minerals and the Mohs reference minerals) was drawn up by the compiler (the VALUES of query 1) and looked up on Wikidata by exact English label (query 1), requesting the instance-of class, chemical formula (P274), Mohs hardness (P1088), Mindat ID (P6263) and Swedish label. Requests were made with Python urllib and curl with the User-Agent "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"; the raw responses were kept in working files (not published), and the queries below reproduce them.

Selection: 40 minerals were kept (see Selection), each a Wikidata item that is an instance of 'mineral species' (Q12089225). For them query 2 fetched every P274 value with its rank, all English and Swedish labels and aliases, and the sv.wikipedia sitelink; query 4 fetched the formula of the related talc item Q108584660 (the mineral item Q134583 has no P274), of andalusite and microcline (named in notes), and the data of chalcocite, arsenopyrite and uraninite, which were added after the first selection.

IMA check: the RRUFF IMA database of mineral properties, suggested as a source, could not be used: rruff.info/ima answered 404, rruff.info redirected to an unrelated NASA database, and the new site's 'IMA Mineral List' page (https://www.rruff.net/ima-mineral-list/) looped in redirects; rruff.net also states only 'Copyright © 2026 RRUFF', so it could only have been a verification source. The official list of the IMA Commission on New Minerals, Nomenclature and Classification, 'The New IMA List of Minerals', updated July 2026, was downloaded as PDF instead (query 6). Its formula column prints sub- and superscripts as smaller characters, so a script (imaformulas.py, a working file, not published; its command line is in query 6) read the characters of each mineral's row with pdfplumber and wrote lowered small characters as subscripts and raised ones as superscripts. All 40 minerals are in the list as valid species.

Formula cross-check: a script (verify.py, a working file, not published; its command line is in query 6) turned each card's formula, each Wikidata P274 value and the IMA formula into element counts (subscript digits read as numbers, oxidation-state superscripts ignored, each element symbol an upper-case letter optionally followed by a lower-case one, parenthesised groups multiplied by the count after them, a hydrate '·2H₂O' added twice) and compared them. All 40 agree in composition with both Wikidata and the IMA list.

Formula notation: the back is Wikidata's P274 string, written with Unicode subscript digits, for 34 minerals; it equals the IMA formula or differs only in brackets the IMA list puts around a single anion group (IMA Ca(CO₃), card CaCO₃; IMA Ca(SO₄)(H₂O)₂, card CaSO₄·2H₂O). For five minerals Wikidata gives the IMA list's structural notation, and the card uses the conventional form of the same composition, as the Swedish Wikipedia and SGU write it: magnetite Fe₃O₄ (IMA and Wikidata Fe²⁺Fe³⁺₂O₄), chromite FeCr₂O₄ (Fe²⁺Cr₂O₄), ilmenite FeTiO₃ (Fe²⁺Ti⁴⁺O₃), orthoclase KAlSi₃O₈ (K(AlSi₃O₈); Wikidata gives KAlSi₃O₈ for microcline) and kyanite Al₂SiO₅ (Al₂OSiO₄; Wikidata gives Al₂SiO₅ for its polymorph andalusite). The notes of magnetite, chromite, ilmenite and kyanite give that structural form, taken from Wikidata's P274 and confirmed by the IMA list. For talc, whose Wikidata mineral item has no formula, the back is the composition of the related Wikidata item Q108584660 (P274 H₂Mg₃O₁₂Si₄, in Hill order) written in conventional mineral notation, Mg₃Si₄O₁₀(OH)₂, which the IMA list and the Swedish Wikipedia confirm. The formula is the ideal (end-member) formula; natural samples vary, which the notes of topaz and sphalerite mention.

Mohs hardness: the ten reference minerals and their numbers were taken from two USGS pages (queries 7 and 8; sources 'usgs-ash' and 'usgs-gemstones'): the volcanic-ash page's table 'Moh's scale of hardness' (1 Talc to 9 Corundum; 6 is 'Orthoclase (Feldspar)') and the 'Natural Gemstones' page ('Talc is 1' to 'Diamond is 10', with 'Feldspar is 6' and 'Sapphire is 9'). They were confirmed by the National Park Service's article (all ten, by the same names, query 9), the Swedish Wikipedia's article 'Mohs hårdhetsskala' (caption listing 1. Talk to 10. Diamant) and Wikidata's P1088 (query 3), which agrees for eight of the ten items; the calcite and apatite discrepancies are recorded under Quality control. The card names the scale's own reference mineral (orthoclase, corundum), as the USGS volcanic-ash page and the NPS article do.

English names: Wikidata's English labels, which match the IMA list's names (its 'Name' column, with the initial capital its explanation describes as table style); the spelling 'baryte' (Wikidata label and IMA name) is used, with 'barite' in the note.

Swedish names: from the Wikidata Swedish label or alias, written in lower case as Swedish common nouns are (capitalised only at the start of a front). Each was resolved on sv.wikipedia through the MediaWiki API, following redirects (query 10): 39 of the 40 reach the item's own article (magnesit redirects to Magnesiumkarbonat, whose article says the compound occurs in nature as magnesit). Each was then looked up in SAOL and SO through the JSON search API behind svenska.se (query 11) and, for ore minerals, in SGU's table 'Några viktiga malmmineral' (query 12) and SGU's 'Handbok för mineraljägare' (query 13). Every name is confirmed by at least two of Wikidata, the Swedish Wikipedia, SAOL/SO and SGU. Where Swedish has two names, the one most sources use was chosen and the other appears in the note or under Quality control: kalkspat (Wikidata label, Swedish Wikipedia, SAOL, SO; SGU writes kalcit), svavelkis (SAOL, SO, Swedish Wikipedia article, Wikidata alias; the Wikidata label is pyrit), järnspat (label, SO, article; SAOL has siderit 'ett järnmineral, järnspat'), fluorit (label, article, SO; flusspat in the note).

Fronts: 'Quartz: chemical formula' / 'Kvarts: kemisk formel' for the 40 formula cards, 'Quartz: Mohs hardness' / 'Kvarts: hårdhet enligt Mohs hårdhetsskala' for the ten hardness cards (the Swedish name of the scale is Wikidata's Swedish label of Q41472 and the Swedish Wikipedia article title). The backs are text in no language (zxx). The deck is studied front to back only, because several formulas belong to more than one mineral (calcite and aragonite CaCO₃, diamond and graphite C) and the hardness numbers are not unique answers in reverse.

Machine checks: every formula card carries a Wikidata check of the P274 value it is based on (the card text itself for 34 cards, otherwise the IMA-style string, and for talc, kyanite and orthoclase the related items above), and a check of the English label and the Swedish label or alias the Swedish name was compared with; the hardness cards check P1088 for the eight items whose Wikidata value is the scale value, and the labels: 150 checks in all, run against live Wikidata by the builder. The deck was built with the builder and validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (node packages/deck-library/scripts/validate_sources.ts minerals).
selection: 40 common minerals: quartz; the carbonates calcite, aragonite, dolomite, magnesite, siderite, malachite and azurite; the halides halite, sylvite and fluorite; the sulfates gypsum, anhydrite and baryte; the sulfides pyrite, galena, sphalerite, chalcopyrite, chalcocite, cinnabar, molybdenite and arsenopyrite; the oxides hematite, magnetite, corundum, cassiterite, rutile, chromite, ilmenite and uraninite; the silicates talc, orthoclase, albite, topaz, zircon, kyanite and beryl; the tungstate scheelite; and the native elements diamond and graphite. They were chosen by the compiler as minerals met in school chemistry and geology: the main rock-forming and ore minerals, the classic evaporites and carbonates, well-known gem minerals and the members of the Mohs scale. Inclusion: an IMA-approved (or grandfathered) valid species with a single ideal formula in the IMA list, a Wikidata item that is a mineral species with that composition, and an established English and Swedish name. The ten Mohs cards cover the scale's complete set of reference minerals (talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz, topaz, corundum, diamond) as published by the USGS; apatite has no formula card because it is a mineral group, not a species. Excluded: groups and series without one formula (feldspar, mica, garnet, olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, apatite, tourmaline); minerals with variable composition written with element ranges, such as pyrrhotite (Fe₁₋ₓS) and wolframite ((Fe,Mn)WO₄); stibnite, whose Swedish name differs between sources (antimonglans in SAOL and SO, antimonit at SGU, spetsglans as the Wikidata label and Swedish Wikipedia title); forsterite and fluorapatite, whose Swedish names have no Swedish Wikipedia article, Wikidata label or dictionary entry to confirm them; and, to keep the deck near 40 minerals, further candidates such as anorthite, microcline, andalusite, muscovite, kaolinite, goethite, cuprite, celestine, cerussite, anglesite, rhodochrosite, smithsonite and wollastonite. Hardness cards are limited to the ten reference minerals: other minerals' hardness is usually a range that varies between sources.

licensing: The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content sources are Wikidata (CC0), for the formulas, names, labels and the selection's lookup, and two US Geological Survey pages, the volcanic-ash hardness table and 'Natural Gemstones' (US federal government works, public domain in the US), for the Mohs reference minerals and their numbers. The selection of the 40 minerals is the compiler's own, and the ten Mohs minerals are the complete set of the scale devised by Friedrich Mohs in 1812 (Wikidata Q41472, inception), shared by every source. The IMA list of minerals (CC BY-SA 3.0), the Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), the National Park Service article (licence uncertain), Svenska Akademiens ordböcker and SGU (all rights reserved) were used for verification only: they confirmed facts that the content sources gave (a mineral's composition, its validity as a species, a Swedish name, a hardness number), and no wording, table or selection was copied from them. The structural forms quoted in four notes are Wikidata's P274 values. The written notation of the formulas, including the conventional forms Fe₃O₄, FeCr₂O₄, FeTiO₃, KAlSi₃O₈, Al₂SiO₅ and Mg₃Si₄O₁₀(OH)₂ that the Swedish Wikipedia and SGU also use, is standard chemical notation of facts, not text taken from those sources. The fronts and notes are the compiler's own wording.

rounds.lens: Sources, licences and machine checks: every formula's composition against Wikidata and the IMA list; every hardness value against two USGS pages, the NPS, Wikidata and the Swedish Wikipedia; every Swedish name against Wikidata, the Swedish Wikipedia, SAOL/SO and SGU.
rounds.scope: All 50 cards, the sources and the deck metadata.
rounds.summary: All 40 formulas agree in composition with Wikidata and the IMA list (July 2026); all ten hardness values agree across the USGS, NPS and Swedish Wikipedia. Wikidata disagrees with the Mohs scale for calcite and apatite; those two P1088 checks were left out and the better-sourced scale values kept. The suggested RRUFF database could not be reached and the official IMA list was used instead. Notation differences and Swedish name choices are recorded below.

findings.issue: Wikidata's calcite item (Q171917) gives Mohs hardness (P1088) 3.04, not 3, the value that defines the scale's step 3 in the USGS pages, the NPS article and the Swedish Wikipedia.
findings.resolution: Back '3' as the scale defines it; no P1088 check on this card (it would fail, and checking a different value would be cherry-picking). Recorded in the card's evidence.

findings.issue: Apatite is a mineral group (Wikidata Q178397, instance of mineral group), and its P1088 is 6 with bounds 5 to 7; the scale's step 5 is apatite in every source (USGS, NPS, Swedish Wikipedia). The species fluorapatite (Q416275) has P1088 5.
findings.resolution: Back '5' as the scale defines it, a note that apatite is a group, no P1088 check; Wikidata's values are quoted in the evidence. Apatite has no formula card.

findings.issue: The USGS gemstones page lists 'Feldspar is 6' and 'Sapphire is 9', naming the group and a variety; the USGS volcanic-ash page lists '6 Orthoclase (Feldspar)' and '9 Corundum', as do the NPS article and Wikidata.
findings.resolution: Cards name orthoclase and corundum, the reference minerals; notes say orthoclase is a feldspar and (on the formula card) that ruby and sapphire are varieties of corundum.

findings.issue: The NPS article's alt text spells the mineral 'Flourite'.
findings.resolution: A typo on that page; the card uses 'Fluorite' as the USGS, the IMA list and Wikidata do. Quoted as printed in the evidence.

findings.issue: The IMA list and Wikidata write magnetite Fe²⁺Fe³⁺₂O₄, chromite Fe²⁺Cr₂O₄, ilmenite Fe²⁺Ti⁴⁺O₃, orthoclase K(AlSi₃O₈) and kyanite Al₂OSiO₄ (structural notation); school chemistry, the Swedish Wikipedia and SGU write Fe₃O₄, FeCr₂O₄, FeTiO₃, KAlSi₃O₈ and Al₂SiO₅.
findings.resolution: The cards use the conventional form, the same composition (checked by script); the notes of magnetite, chromite, ilmenite and kyanite give the IMA form. The Wikidata checks of these five cards check the IMA-style P274 string the card is based on, and for orthoclase and kyanite also microcline's KAlSi₃O₈ and andalusite's Al₂SiO₅.

findings.issue: The Wikidata mineral item talc (Q134583) has no chemical formula (P274).
findings.resolution: Composition taken from the related Wikidata item Q108584660 (talc, P274 H₂Mg₃O₁₂Si₄ in Hill order) and written in the mineral form Mg₃Si₄O₁₀(OH)₂, which is the IMA formula and what the Swedish Wikipedia gives; the check is on Q108584660's P274.

findings.issue: The IMA list brackets single anion groups (Ca(CO₃), Ba(SO₄), Zr(SiO₄), Be₃Al₂(Si₆O₁₈)) and writes gypsum Ca(SO₄)(H₂O)₂; Wikidata writes CaCO₃, BaSO₄, ZrSiO₄, Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈ and CaSO₄·2H₂O.
findings.resolution: Cards follow Wikidata's conventional strings (and the brief's examples SiO₂, CaCO₃); compositions are identical.

findings.issue: RRUFF's IMA database, which the brief suggested, was unreachable on 2026-10-04 (rruff.info/ima 404; rruff.info redirects to an unrelated NASA site; rruff.net's IMA list page loops in redirects) and is 'Copyright © 2026 RRUFF' without an open licence. Mindat, also suggested, was not consulted: the official IMA list it derives its approved formulas from was available and sufficient.
findings.resolution: The CNMNC's own IMA list (July 2026, CC BY-SA 3.0) was used for verification. No content was taken from RRUFF or Mindat.

findings.issue: Swedish has two names for calcite: kalkspat (Wikidata label, Swedish Wikipedia article title, SAOL, SO and the Swedish Wikipedia's Mohs caption) and kalcit (SGU's usage, a Wikidata alias; the Swedish Wikipedia article says 'Kalkspat även kallat kalcit'; not in SAOL or SO).
findings.resolution: kalkspat, the name in the dictionaries and the label; recorded here.

findings.issue: The Wikidata Swedish label is 'pyrit', but SAOL has only 'svavelkis', SO refers 'pyrit' to 'svavelkis', and the Swedish Wikipedia article is 'Svavelkis'.
findings.resolution: Front 'Svavelkis'; note 'Kallas även pyrit eller kattguld'; the check is on the Wikidata alias 'svavelkis'.

findings.issue: SGU's table writes zinkblände as (Zn, Fe)S, the natural composition; the IMA formula and Wikidata give ZnS.
findings.resolution: Back ZnS (ideal formula); the note says natural sphalerite usually contains some iron, as the Swedish Wikipedia also states.
